research_question: What is the effect of an implantable gentamicin-collagen sponge placed in the sternotomy wound, compared with no topical antimicrobial, on superficial surgical site infection (SSI) in adults undergoing cardiac surgery?
control_label: No topical antimicrobial (routine care or placebo)
outcome_description: Incidence of superficial sternal surgical site infection (SSI) within 30 to 90 days postoperatively
positive_direction: Reduced risk of superficial surgical site infection favoring the gentamicin-collagen sponge group
search_queries: gentamicin collagen sponge sternotomy superficial surgical site infection trial
gentamicin impregnated collagen implant cardiac surgery sternal wound infection randomized
gentamicin fleece sternal infection controlled comparison cardiac surgery
inclusion_criteria: Adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery involving median sternotomy
Intervention arm receiving an implantable gentamicin-collagen sponge/fleece placed in the sternal wound during closure
Reports quantitative incidence of superficial surgical site infection (SSI) for both intervention and control arms
exclusion_criteria: Not an original empirical study (systematic reviews, meta-analyses, narrative reviews, editorials, comments, or theoretical papers)
No comparison between an implantable gentamicin-collagen sponge and a control group without topical antimicrobial
No quantitative outcome data reported specifically for superficial surgical site infection (e.g., only reporting total SSI or deep SSI/mediastinitis without superficial SSI breakdown)
Completely unrelated to cardiac surgery or sternotomy procedures in adults
moderators_to_extract: Type of cardiac surgery (isolated CABG vs. mixed/valve surgery)
Number or dose of gentamicin-collagen sponges used
Study design (blinded RCT vs. open-label RCT vs. prospective controlled trial)
Sternal closure technique (e.g., standard wire vs. rigid fixation)
effect_size_note: Extracted as dichotomous event counts (number of superficial surgical site infections and total patients per arm) and pooled as Risk Ratio (RR).
